questions.q: In NumPy, what does the `*` operator do between two 2-D arrays (matrices)?
options: Standard matrix multiplication
Elementwise multiplication of corresponding entries
The dot product, returning a single scalar
It raises an error for any 2-D arrays
questions.explain: `*` always performs elementwise multiplication in NumPy. True matrix multiplication (and matrix-vector or dot-product multiplication) uses the `@` operator instead.

questions.q: Why is np.linalg.solve(A, b) generally preferred over np.linalg.inv(A) @ b for solving Ax = b?
options: solve() gives a different, more accurate answer mathematically
solve() is faster and more numerically stable, since explicitly forming the inverse amplifies rounding error
inv() cannot be used with the @ operator
solve() does not require A to be square
questions.explain: Both approaches are mathematically equivalent, but solve() uses an internal factorization (like LU) that avoids the extra numerical error introduced by explicitly computing A inverse.

questions.q: When should you use np.linalg.eigh(A) instead of np.linalg.eig(A)?
options: Only when A is a 1x1 matrix
When A is known to be symmetric, since eigh guarantees real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors
eigh and eig always return identical results in all cases, so it never matters
Only when A has a zero determinant
questions.explain: eigh is specialized for symmetric (or Hermitian) matrices and exploits that structure to guarantee real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, unlike the general-purpose eig.

questions.q: For a matrix A that is NOT square, which decomposition can still be computed directly?
options: Eigendecomposition via np.linalg.eig
Cholesky decomposition
Singular value decomposition via np.linalg.svd
None of these work for non-square matrices
questions.explain: The SVD is defined for any real matrix regardless of shape, unlike eigendecomposition and Cholesky decomposition, which both require a square matrix.

questions.q: For a symmetric positive definite matrix A, how do the eigenvalues from eigh(A) relate to the singular values from svd(A)?
options: They are unrelated numbers
They are exactly the same set of numbers, just typically returned in opposite sort order (ascending vs descending)
Eigenvalues are always twice the singular values
Singular values are always zero for symmetric matrices
questions.explain: For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the eigenvalues and singular values coincide exactly; eigh conventionally returns them ascending while svd returns them descending.
